Don't touch anyone's tail. I can't believe I have to say this, but you've got that look.
If you've got #food# on you, share it before anyone asks. Asking is rude, and then we'd have to be rude back.
place:wild: Stay on the road, {you}. Everything that goes wrong out here starts with someone saying 'shortcut'.
Get your fire lit before dark, and put your back against something that isn't a tree.
Moving water only. If it's still, something's keeping it still.
Slimes are slow, goblins are stupid, and wolves are neither. Save your running for the wolves.
If you hear horns, get off the road. If the sky goes rust, get under something.
Never sleep where you cook. You'd think that was obvious. There are graves out here that say otherwise.
Carry more food than you need. Out here you're either the one with the bread or the one looking for someone with bread.
Those mountains look close. They aren't. Anything that looks close out here is lying.
The further you get from a wall, the less a Law can do for you. Out here it's just you and whoever's bigger.
When in doubt, look for smoke. A chimney's straight, and a campfire means someone else is lost too.
#saying# Out here, that's worth more than a sword.
Don't stop for anyone near #far_place#, not even if they ask nicely. Especially if they ask nicely.
If you meet #beast#, you walk. You don't run, you walk. I learned that from #relative#, and it's the only reason I'm here.
about:human: {place} is a farming village of crooked fences and long memories, where the best gossip is traded at the well.
{place} sits among barley fields, its one road worn deep by carts and by people leaving for somewhere better.
The bell in {place} has been slightly flat for ninety years, and the village has come to consider this a point of pride.
{place} has a Guild hall too big for its needs, built in a hopeful year and never quite forgiven.
Half the houses in {place} have been rebuilt at least once, and you can read the old raids in the colour of the stone.
{place} is the sort of village where a stranger's arrival is still discussed at funerals.
Smoke, chickens and a stream that floods every spring: {place} has never asked for more, and has rarely got it.
{place} grows more onions than it can eat and more opinions than it can use.
The people of {place} mend everything twice, throw nothing away, and know exactly who owes whom for what.
{place} looks peaceful from the road, which is why the watchtower at its edge is the first thing anyone builds back.
about:city: {place} rises behind grey walls, loud with hammers and hawkers, smelling of bread, tar and other people's money.
Everything has a price in {place}, and a clerk to write it down, and a second clerk to watch the first.
{place} is a city of narrow streets and wide ambitions, where the watch walks in pairs and the rats in regiments.
The walls of {place} have been raised three times, and every generation has been told that this height is the last.
{place} never quite sleeps: when the taverns close the bakers start, and the gates open on the smell of both.
In {place} the market square is older than the keep and has, by most accounts, overthrown it twice.
Golems stand at the crossroads of {place}, and its citizens have learned to commit their sins indoors.
{place} has four hundred years of grudges and one very good fish stew.
Banners hang from every tower in {place}, each one faded by a different war.
A stranger can lose a purse, a day or a whole self in {place}, and the city will charge for all three.
about:elf: {place} is built so gently into the forest that a traveller can walk through it without knowing, which the elves consider good manners.
Lanterns of pale glass hang among the boughs of {place}, and they were burning before the kingdom had a name.
The houses of {place} are grown, not built, and each one is still slowly making up its mind.
In {place} a conversation may last a season, and the moss has been known to finish people's sentences.
{place} smells of rain and old bark, and nothing in it has ever been in a hurry.
The elves of {place} keep a record of every storm for nine hundred years, and file their grudges alongside.
Silver-barked trees ring {place}, and the rangers say they can tell an honest visitor by how the leaves turn.
{place} is so quiet that newcomers can hear their own hearts, and the locals politely pretend they can't.
The footpaths in {place} move a little from year to year, following the roots.
Time seems to pool in {place}, the way water does in a hollow stone.
about:elfcity: {place} climbs the great tree in tier upon tier of living wood, its bridges swaying high above the forest floor.
The towers of {place} were not raised but persuaded, over many centuries, from the branches of the Elder Tree.
{place} glows faintly at dusk, when ten thousand lanterns wake among its leaves.
{place} has stood in the arms of the Elder Tree since before the Law, and of late its highest leaves have begun to thin.
In {place} every stair is a root and every wall a branch, and the whole city creaks in the wind like a ship at anchor.
The court of {place} has been in continuous session for longer than most kingdoms have existed.
Music drifts down through {place} at all hours, and nobody living can say when it began.
A human could spend a lifetime in {place} and be regarded, at the end of it, as a recent arrival.
Nothing in {place} has a straight line, a sharp corner or any intention of explaining itself.
The great halls of {place} are older than the written word, and they resent it.
about:beast: {place} is a ring of hide tents and cook-fires on the open grass, where every argument is settled loudly and then forgotten over meat.
The drums of {place} can be heard a day's walk away, and they usually mean dinner.
{place} moves a little with the seasons, and the only thing that stays put is the chief's fire.
Bones and bright cloth hang from the poles of {place}, each one marking a hunt or a wedding, and sometimes both.
In {place} a stranger is judged by grip and appetite, and the judges are very thorough.
The wind never stops in {place}, and neither does the laughter, which is mostly aimed at visitors.
{place} sits where the grass meets the red rock, and its people have been fighting orcs there for as long as anyone has told stories.
Children in {place} can track a hare before they can count, and they see no reason to learn the second.
{place} has no walls, on the grounds that walls are for those who can't run or can't fight.
Every fire in {place} has a story that goes with it, and none of them is short.
mission:arrive: If the sky really dropped you here, I'd go and see King {king} in {capital}. He's the only one with enough titles to do anything about it.
You'll want {capital}, {you}. Follow the road till the walls get big. King {king} has been asking after someone like you.
Advice? Go to {capital}, see King {king}, and don't eat anything from the stalls by the gate.
Anyone with a sword and a purpose ends up in front of King {king} sooner or later. {capital}'s not far. Save yourself the detour.
I'm the wrong person to ask. King {king} is the right one. He's in {capital}, in the big house with all the guards.
They say the King's been waiting on someone. If it's you, you're late, and I'd start walking to {capital}.
Talk to the King. {king} isn't a fool, whatever they say in {capital}, and he's the only one who can open the right doors.
Everything in {kingdom} goes through {capital} eventually. Taxes, soldiers, bad news. Go and join it. King {king} will see you.
#saying# And after that, I'd go straight to {capital} and see King {king}, because I've got nothing else for you.
mission:oaths: The elves, is it? Take a long book and a longer patience. And bring something shiny from the mountains. They say the Tree's been hungry.
You'll not talk the tribes round with words, {you}. Go south and east, and take something to hit with.
The sea folk haven't spoken to anyone on land since that harbour business. If I were you, I'd ask {second_ruler} in {second_city} what we did.
The Crown's the easy one. Do the Guild's dirty work a while and the King'll come round. He's fair, as kings go.
Elves are west, where the trees start looking at you. They'll tell you no for a century. Don't take it personally.
I had it from #relative#: the beastkin don't swear on paper. They swear on what you've done with your hands.
If it's mermaids you're after, learn to hold your breath, and learn to apologise. I don't know which is harder.
The Guild will vouch for anyone who finishes a job and doesn't steal the spoons. That'll get you the Crown, at least.
The tribes? Start at {beast_village}, where the grass gets tall and the people get loud. Eat everything they hand you.
The elves will send you to {elf_capital}, and {elf_title} {elf_ruler} will look at you as if you were weather.
mission:ruins: The old ruins? South, past the last of the tribes' fires. I've only ever met one person who went, and she came back and took up knitting.
Nobody goes that far south, {you}. That's not advice, it's a fact. The beastkin will point the way, and then they'll stop walking.
There's a cairn down there, they say, older than the tribes or younger, depending who's drunk. Take water.
The ruins are in the Wilds, far south. Whoever stacked those stones wanted to be found, by my reckoning, or they'd have picked somewhere nice.
Ask a beastkin scout about the southern ruins and watch their ears go flat. It's a long walk, and nobody likes to talk about it.
If you're going south, go in daylight and go alone. Nobody'll go with you anyway.
Head for the hot country, past the last fires, and keep walking after it's stopped making sense. That's how I heard it.
A trader told me there's writing in the ruins nobody can read. He said it as if that were a good thing. Bring a lamp.
Take #food#, and more than you think you need. There's nothing to eat past the last fires, and nothing out there's hungry, which worries me.
mission:confess: If you've got a question for {god}, ask it straight. I've always found the sky answers better when you stop being polite.
You've got a face on you like someone who's been lied to. In my experience, you go and ask them. Even if it's a {godkind}.
Talk to {god}, then. Out loud, on your own, wherever you are. The priests want you to think there's a fee, and there isn't.
I don't know what you found out, {you}, and I don't want to. But if someone owes you the truth, make them say it to your face.
My mother used to say, ask a {godkind} a small question and you get a sermon. Ask a big one and you get silence. So wait. Silence gets uncomfortable.
Whoever you're angry at, tell them. You look like you've been carrying something up a hill.
Sometimes the only one who knows is the one who won't say. You sit there until they do. It's how I got the truth out of #relative#.

stone:cairn: A cairn of flat stones, stacked by someone who cared more about it staying up than looking good. The carving on its face is deep, patient and truly ugly.

The letters are worn shallow in one place, where a thumb has traced them over and over. It would have had to be the same thumb.
There's no moss on the carving, though there's moss on everything else. Even the weather seems to be leaving it alone.
The stones are warm from the sun, and that's all they are. You stand there a little longer than you need to.
Low on the back of the cairn, easy to miss, someone has scratched a small, badly drawn bus.

stone:law_stone: The stone hums in your teeth and gives you nothing. It was never going to answer one voice. It answers four peoples, speaking as one.

These letters were cut by someone who knew what they meant. You have the uneasy feeling that someone still does, and has been hoping you won't ask.
Nothing happens. Whatever is asked here has to be asked with the whole truth in hand, and {god} is the one holding the rest of it.
